title: Bodhisattva Methods, Part 4: Identity Action
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The main teaching of the Soto Zen dharma talk is that meditation practice can help us cultivate mindfulness, awareness, and balance in our lives, allowing us to navigate both challenging and joyful experiences with greater ease and connection to ourselves and others. By embracing this paradoxical nature of life, we can learn to be more adaptable, humble, and kind, even in difficult situations, and find a sense of completion and wholeness through our spiritual practice. Ultimately, the goal is not to achieve a fixed state, but to cultivate a fluid and dynamic awareness that allows us to move with greater harmony and compassion in the world.
topics: Dogen's Bodhisattva's Four Methods of Guidance

It sounds almost clinical sometimes, the way Zen is portrayed, but I think when you really put these two sides of human experience and these two qualities of practice together, it's really more about connection, aliveness, and love, and love.

Remember, the first of the four methods for how to practice in this way, as a person devoted to awakening, devoted to Bodhi, Bodhisattva, is the practice of giving.
And he reminds us to have a very wide view of what giving is and can be.
Not to focus too much on whether we're giving the right things or giving enough stuff, or doing it right, doing it wrong.
Not to focus so much on the thing as an object and the person receiving as another object, but to focus on the practice of giving.

He says:

This will be a wholesome seed for this and other lifetimes.
Give your valuables.
Give a penny.
Give a blade of grass.
This will be a wholesome root for this and other lifetimes.
The truth will turn into valuables.
The valuables will turn into truth.*

The last of his four methods is really interesting.

I fear we'd better touch on the first three or we wouldn't know what he's talking about.
The last of his four methods, and this feels like one of the teachings and understandings that are really given as a gift to humanity, he calls identity action.
So it has to do with the skillful use of identification.

The Bodhisattva is perfectly as willing to clean the toilet as she is to give the Dharma talk or officiate at the service or fix the website or help somebody with their car.
The Bodhisattva steps into the role that's most helpful in a way that is often quiet, often unselfconscious.
And therefore the Bodhisattva is also able to step out of that role when it's no longer helpful.
And here's where we often fall down, though.

We get really good at our role, and maybe our role has some very wise and altruistic aspects to it, and maybe it made a lot of sense five years ago, or ten years ago, or twenty years ago, but here we are.
Here we are, maybe ignoring the ways that we have changed, the ways that people around us have changed.

We start to see, oh, she's changed.
I've changed.
I don't have to play this role anymore and can change to something else.

Here's what Dogen says about this identity action.
This willingness to meet the world in a strong way, a dignified way, and a skillful way.
What form should I take?
That's what he means.
Dogen wrote:
*Action means the right form with dignity and correct manner.
This means that you cause yourself to be in identity with others, causing others to be in identity with you.
However, the relationship of self and others varies limitlessly according to circumstances.*
Maybe I should have just said that for the whole talk, sorry.
Let's unpack it just a little bit.
*Action means right form, dignity, and the right form.
This means that you cause yourself to be in identity with others after causing others to be in identity with you.

So no one way, right?

We're called upon to get over ourselves or rise out of some perceived limitation, to work with some fear, some limit that we've placed on ourselves.

But Dogen paints an even bigger picture, because he says in his poetic way, using mountains, that if we don't cooperate with identity action, there's a way the whole world is going to be a little akimbo, a little messed up.
He says:
*The ocean, mountains and water, the ocean does not refuse to be water.
That's why it's so large.*
Think about it, the ocean is like, I don't want to be water, you know?
Not today.
*The mountain does not refuse the soil.
That's why it is high.
A wise lord does not exclude people.
That's why he has many subjects.
This being so, water comes together to form the ocean.
Soil piles up to form the mountains because the mountains do not refuse to be mountains.
They are mountains and they are high because the lord is not weary of the people, the people assemble.*
Presumably the people have joy.
So it's not just for our own benefit that we practice identity action, but so that the whole world can be in more harmony.
So I guess I'll have to save [unclear: "Ren's"] book for next time.
I think I'll close with another story.
There's some great stories in here, very realistic stories about practicing with identity action in the monastery, which basically means that she was upset a lot.
It was difficult.
I'll tell you more about that.

Beautiful too.

He told the story of a French surrealist poet who was active in the thirties and forties named Robert Desnos.
Half Jewish, and he stayed in France, in South France in the Vichy.

So they're being transported somewhere.
Leaving the barracks the mood is somber because everyone knows that the truck is headed for the gas chamber.
And when the truck arrives no one can speak.
Even the guards fall silent.
But this silence is soon interrupted by an energetic man who jumps into the line and grabs one of the condemned.
Improbable as it is, my friend told me, Desnos the poet starts to read this man's poem.
Oh, he says, I see you have a very long lifeline and you're going to have three children.
He's exuberant and his excitement is contagious.
First one man and then another offers up his hand to be read, and the prediction each time is for longevity, more children and abundant joy.
As Desnos reads more poems, not only does the mood of the prisoners change but that of the guards too.
How can one explain it?
Perhaps the element of surprise has planted a shadow of doubts in their mind.
If they told themselves these deaths were inevitable, they no longer seem inevitable.
And they are in any case so disoriented by the sudden change of mood amongst those that they were about to kill that they're unable to go through with the execution.
So all the men along with Desnos are packed back in the truck and taken back to the barracks.
Desnos has saved his own life in the lives of the others by using his imagination.*
I was thinking not just imagination, but there's an example, maybe a sort of wild example, of this identity action.
Somehow he intuited a role.
You have the role of waiting in line to be murdered, or you can take up this role of the exuberant palm reader.
Unbelievable.
I don't know if there's historical documentation that this really happened or not, but it's a story that's been told I guess since that time.
But sadly, Robert Desnos, he did survive the war, the camp was liberated, but a couple of days later he died of typhus.

But they allow us to engage this world, to move between what sometimes in Buddhism they call the absolute, this world of peace, completion, and the relative world, the world of turmoil and change and joy and sadness, a little more fluidly.
Maybe one day supporting us and being able to jump off the truck and start reading poems, or whatever else it is that the world asks of us.

I hope you appreciated those thoughts.

Remember them all?

So basically three variations on giving, and how do we identify?
